svg.aria-label: Training and pruning fruit trees. Basic cuts: heading back shortens a shoot to force new shoots; thinning removes a branch at its base to reduce the number of branches; cutting back removes part of an older limb to renew it; leaving a shoot unpruned promotes fruiting. A heading cut is made about 0.5-1 cm above a bud, sloping away from the bud; the bud below the cut faces outwards so the new shoot grows outwards and the crown opens; a stub left too long dies back into a dead snag where disease gets in; a cut too close to the bud makes the bud dry out. A thinning cut is made flush with the collar at the base of the branch, leaving no stub but not cutting into the trunk; cuts and saw cuts over about 2 cm across are pared smooth and coated with wax, paint or clay. Branches over about 5 cm across are removed with three cuts: first saw up from below about 1/3 of the way through, about 20-30 cm beyond the final cut; then a few cm further out saw down from above until the branch falls; finally cut off the stub flush with the collar. Common tree forms: open centre, trunk about 40-60 cm high, no central leader, 3 main limbs about 120° apart, staggered about 10-20 cm vertically, at about 40-60° to the horizontal, 2-3 laterals on each main limb, tree about 2.5-3 m tall, used for peach, plum, apricot and others; tiered form with a central leader, 5-7 main limbs in 2-3 tiers, 3 in the first tier, 2 in the second and 1-2 in the third, tiers about 80-100 cm apart, tree about 4-5 m tall, takes 4-6 years to form, used for standard apple trees, pear, persimmon, walnut and chestnut; spindle, 10-20 smaller branches spiralling round one upright central leader, tied down to about 70-90° from the leader or even drooping, longer below and shorter above, tree about 2.5-3.5 m tall, used for dwarf high-density apple and pear.
svg.title: Pruning fruit trees: cuts and common tree forms

g.text: Pruning fruit trees: cuts and common tree forms
Winter pruning (after leaf fall, before buds break in spring) is mostly thinning, heading back
and cutting back; it decides next year's tree shape and crop
Large before small, top before bottom, inside before outside;
remove dead, diseased or pest-damaged, crossing, overlapping and inward-growing branches and water shoots
⑤ Where to make a heading cut
Wounds: pare cuts and saw cuts over about 2 cm across smooth, then coat with wax, paint, or yellow clay
mixed with a little cow dung, to stop cracking and disease getting in
⑥ Thinning cut: flush with the collar
Collar: the slightly raised ring at the base
of a branch. Cut flush with it: leave no
stub, but do not cut into the trunk
⑦ Branches over ~5 cm: three cuts
① About 20-30 cm beyond the final cut, saw
up from below about 1/3 of the way through
② A few cm further out than ①, saw down
from above until the branch drops
③ Last, cut the stub off flush with the
(side view, same scale; winter framework after leaf fall)
between tiers let light into the
ones a bit longer, upper shorter;
any branch over half as thick as
the leader: remove and replace it
